question: What is the primary site for nutrient absorption in the human body?
explanation: The small intestine has specialized structures that provide a massive surface area specifically designed for taking in digested nutrients. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T7#GNS121_U1_T7_h1)

question: Where do most absorbed nutrients go immediately after leaving the digestive tract?

options.A: Back into the stomach for further breakdown
options.B: Through the portal vein to the liver
options.C: Directly to the kidneys for filtration

explanation: Great job thinking through this! Blood from the intestines travels straight through the hepatic portal system to the liver first so it can process all those fresh nutrients before they circulate everywhere else.

question: What do we call the tiny, microscopic projections found right on the surface of intestinal lining cells?
explanation: Spot on! Microvilli sit right on top of the intestinal cells, forming a 'brush border' that gives an amazing boost to the surface area available for absorbing food.

question: Why does the small intestine have folds, villi, and microvilli along its inner lining?

options.A: To speed up the movement of waste through the gut
options.B: To prevent bacteria from entering the bloodstream
options.C: To increase the surface area for absorbing nutrients
options.D: To produce strong muscular contractions for vomiting

explanation: You've got this! These tiny folds and projections multiply the inner space of the small intestine so your body can capture as many nutrients as possible.

question: Which type of nutrient transport across cell membranes requires the body to use energy (ATP)?
explanation: Well done! Just like carrying a heavy load uphill, active transport needs a little boost of cellular energy (ATP) to push nutrients where they need to go.

question: What is the main difference between simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion?

options.A: Simple diffusion moves nutrients against a gradient, while facilitated moves with it
options.B: Simple diffusion only moves water, while facilitated diffusion moves solids
options.C: Simple diffusion requires ATP, while facilitated diffusion does not
options.D: Simple diffusion does not use carrier proteins, while facilitated diffusion does

explanation: Think of simple diffusion as slipping easily through a gap, while facilitated diffusion needs special protein 'doorkeepers' to help molecules across the membrane.

question: Into what smaller forms must dietary proteins be broken down before they can be absorbed?
explanation: Proteins are usually too bulky to pass through the gut wall as they are, so digestive enzymes break them down into tiny building blocks like amino acids first.

question: A patient has a blockage in their intestinal lymph vessels (lacteals). Which nutrient absorption will be hit hardest?
explanation: Remember that dietary fats are too chunky for regular blood capillaries, so they get packaged and sent straight into the lymphatic lacteals instead!

question: Which specific vitamin needs a special helper protein called 'intrinsic factor' from the stomach to be absorbed properly?
explanation: Intrinsic factor is like a VIP escort for Vitamin B12! It teams up in the stomach to protect the vitamin until they reach the lower part of the small intestine for absorption.

question: What actually drives water to move passively across the wall of the intestine?

options.A: Active water pumps on the enterocyte membrane
options.C: Direct muscle contractions of the villi
options.D: Osmotic gradients created by solute absorption

explanation: Water loves to follow the crowd! As the gut pumps in salts and sugars, water naturally flows right along with them through osmosis.

question: What usually happens if food travels through the small intestine much faster than normal?

options.A: Increased vitamin storage in the liver
options.C: Higher than normal blood sugar spikes

explanation: When food rushes through too fast, digestive enzymes and cells don't get enough time to do their job, leaving unabsorbed nutrients to pull extra water into the stool.

question: Which of these options has NO effect on how well your body absorbs nutrients?

options.A: The health and integrity of the villi
options.B: The pH of the digestive tract
options.D: The astrological sign of the patient

explanation: Haha, definitely not your horoscope! Nutrient absorption depends strictly on physical and chemical factors like gut movement, pH, and mucosal health.

question: What is the medical term for pale, greasy, and very foul-smelling stools caused by fats that weren't absorbed?
explanation: When fats escape digestion and absorption, they show up in the waste, giving stool that classic pale, oily, and heavy-smelling look known as steatorrhea.

question: A patient with long-term malabsorption shows up with easy bruising and bleeding gums. Which vitamin deficiency is the likely culprit?
explanation: Spot on! Fat-soluble vitamins like Vitamin K need healthy fat absorption to enter the body. Without it, clotting factors drop, leading to easy bruising and bleeding.
